transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Time: 16:30 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Aisha Patel (Redwood AE), Lucas Mendes (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Silverpine - Head of ML), Carlos Ruiz (Silverpine - Eng Manager), Sophie Lee (Silverpine - Security), Tom Novak (Silverpine - Data Eng)

Summary:
Quick hosted API walkthrough focused on chat/text generation basics: streaming, key parameters, and how retries/backoff should be handled in client code. Security and next steps for a pilot were discussed.

Topics covered:
- Hosted API quickstart + console demo
- Streaming vs non-streaming responses and how to parse partial chunks
- Important params: max_tokens, temperature, top_p, stop sequences, presence/penalty
- Retry semantics, idempotency keys, and recommended backoff strategy
- Rate limiting, batching and cost/latency tradeoffs
- Security questions: SOC 2, KMS, SSO/SAML, data retention

Transcript body:
[00:00] Aisha Patel: hey everyone thanks for joining, we're gonna run through the hosted API demo for chat and text generation basics. lucas will do the demo and i'll answer process questions.
[00:12] Maya Chen: thanks aisha, quick heads up we mostly care about streaming responses for our chat UI and handling retries from the browser side so interested in how you recommend doing that.
[00:23] Lucas Mendes: cool, i'll share my screen — first quick note on endpoints: we have a /v1/chat/completions style endpoint for chat and a /v1/generate for single-turn text, both support streaming. streaming is server-sent events style, chunked json so you parse incremental tokens.
[00:40] Carlos Ruiz: is that SSE or websockets? we have websocket infra but prefer SSE in our frontend.
[00:47] Lucas Mendes: primarily SSE and also streaming-over-http with chunked tokens — works fine with fetch and eventsource. some clients e.g. old IE need polyfills. sorry typo earlier i called it "sse stream mix" — it's basically chunked json events.
[01:07] Sophie Lee: on security, does the streaming connection ever leak partial logs to third parties? how's that audited?
[01:15] Aisha Patel: good q — audit logs are in the console; streaming payloads go over TLS, and we keep request/response logs per request id. we can provide SOC2 docs and our KMS integration notes.
[01:30] Lucas Mendes: jumping into params — you set max_tokens to cap generation length, temperature for randomness (0.0 deterministic to ~1.0 more random), top_p for nucleus sampling, stop sequences to terminate early. also you can supply system/user roles in chat arrays.
[01:55] Tom Novak: curious about cost implications — if we set temperature high or use longer max_tokens, obviously cost goes up, but are there any perf impacts?
[02:05] Lucas Mendes: perf is mostly tokens generated; latency per token is stable but longer outputs increase end-to-end latency. batching and prefix caching reduce per-token cost on our side; hosted routing will try to match workload to a cost/perf profile — examples we'll send in the pricing sheet.
[02:28] Maya Chen: can you demo streaming with cancellation? our UI cancels mid-response when users click stop.
[02:34] Lucas Mendes: yep — demo now. (screen) making a chat call in streaming mode... you see partial chunks arrive, we append them client-side; if you cancel we send a connection close and we recommend also POSTing an idempotency key for retryable operations so you don't double-charge. note: the idempotency key is primarily for non-streamed create-like operations, but you can pair it with server-side request ids. 
[03:12] Carlos Ruiz: what about retries — if our client gets a 5xx mid-stream, should we retry from scratch or resume?
[03:20] Lucas Mendes: short answer: restart from scratch is simplest. we don't support resume of partial token streams today for hosted endpoints. recommended pattern: set a short backoff with exponential backoff + jitter, include the same conversation context and idempotency key to prevent duplicate side effects, and use dedupe on your application layer for events. we'll include a sample retry helper in the repo.
[03:52] Sophie Lee: is there a maximum recognized for rate limits? we need per-user rate limiting and burst protection.
[03:58] Aisha Patel: yes we have tiered rate limits by plan and API keys; for enterprise we can provision dedicated pools or increase rate limits. dedicated/reserved capacity (Redwood Dedicated) is an option if you need predictable throughput.
[04:20] Maya Chen: you mentioned prefix caching earlier — what does that mean?
[04:25] Lucas Mendes: prefix caching stores KV cache entries for repeated prompts or system messages so subsequent requests that reuse prefixes can reuse KV cache. it can reduce token generation time and cost. sometimes i say "KV cache" or i mis-say "KV cash" in demos — that was me earlier, sorry.
[04:40] Tom Novak: nice. what's the typical latency per token for hosted?
[04:45] Lucas Mendes: depends on model and sequence length — for smaller models you can see 20–40ms per token, larger models 60–120ms; we'll send model-specific p50/p95 numbers. streaming amortizes latency for UIs.
[05:05] Maya Chen: do you support function calling / structured outputs? we use tool calls to fetch data.
[05:11] Lucas Mendes: yes, we have structured output support and function/tool calling in chat. function-calling acts like an instrumented call and you can capture tool outputs. a quick demo later if you want an extra session.
[05:33] Carlos Ruiz: logging and retention — how long are conversation logs kept? and is data used to train models?
[05:40] Aisha Patel: by default hosted logs are retained 30 days for debugging; enterprise customers can request different retention and data-handling terms. we don't use customer data to train open models unless there's explicit opt-in — it's in the security whitepaper. sophie we should send the exact policy.
[06:00] Sophie Lee: yes please, and specifics on KMS/HSM for key management.
[06:06] Lucas Mendes: quick note on retries again — client should treat streaming as non-idempotent (since partial outputs might have been delivered). for operations that cause side effects we recommend an idempotency token with server-side dedupe. for pure generation (no side effects) retrying is ok but you'll get potentially different outputs unless temperature is 0 or you seed determinism.
[06:35] Maya Chen: can you show sample code for streaming in JS?
[06:40] Lucas Mendes: sure — showing fetch with ReadableStream, parsing chunks and applying backpressure, example repo link: github.com/redwood-inference/examples/streaming-chat (note: link may be truncated in transcript).
[07:02] Carlos Ruiz: earlier you mentioned rate-limits and quotas per key — is there a per-model concurrency limit?
[07:08] Aisha Patel: concurrency limits are per-account/plan and we expose those in the console. for high-volume customers we do dedicated capacity with explicit concurrency guarantees.
[07:25] Tom Novak: what about client-side SDK retries vs server side? what does Redwood recommend?
[07:30] Lucas Mendes: recommend client-side exponential backoff with jitter for transient 5xx and network errors, and server returns Retry-After for rate-limit (429). we also recommend circuit-breaker if you see sustained errors. sample client code in repo handles these.
[07:50] Maya Chen: about tokenization — do you provide token counts before sending so we can estimate cost and enforce limits client-side?
[07:58] Aisha Patel: we provide tokenization utilities in SDK and you can request a token-usage estimate; the console also shows per-request token counts in logs.
[08:12] Lucas Mendes: demo: sending a chat payload with streaming enabled, temperature 0.7, max_tokens 150 — showing partial output in the UI and how to wire stop sequences. (visual)
[08:42] Maya Chen: this looks good. any caveats for mobile clients with flaky connectivity?
[08:48] Lucas Mendes: for mobile, shorter timeouts, handle reconnection, and design your UI to show partial drafts and make generation restartable. also consider server-side caching of previous contexts for quicker warm starts.
[09:12] Carlos Ruiz: are there SDKs for python/node?
[09:16] Aisha Patel: yes official SDKs for python and node with streaming helpers; community SDKs exist too.
[09:28] Sophie Lee: would we need a private deployment (VPC/on-prem) to meet our compliance, or can hosted cover SOC2 + customer-managed KMS?
[09:36] Aisha Patel: many enterprise customers start with hosted + customer-managed KMS + contractually agreed retention. if you need VPC or air-gapped on-prem, that's our Redwood Private offering, which has different timelines and licensing. we'll map that in the security doc.
[09:55] Maya Chen: timeline: we want to pilot in 4–6 weeks if possible, what do you need from us?
[10:02] Aisha Patel: ideal next steps: we need sample prompts, expected qps, success metrics, and security checklist. we'll send pricing and sandbox keys and Lucas will provide a benchmark script for your traffic pattern.
[10:20] Lucas Mendes: question from transcript: i sometimes say product names off — "Redwood Runtime" is the serving runtime, "Redwood Dedicated" is reserved capacity. apologies for any slurred names.
[10:33] Tom Novak: any competitor concerns we should be aware of? we evaluated OpenAI and some self-hosting options.
[10:40] Aisha Patel: common tradeoffs: OpenAI is simple and has broad models, self-hosting gives control but has ops cost. Redwood focuses on predictable latency/cost and unified ops across hosted/dedicated/private. we'll include a short comparison doc.
[10:58] Maya Chen: ok let's recap and next steps.
[11:02] Aisha Patel: recap: we'll send pricing sheet, SOC2 & KMS docs, sandbox API key, and a sample streaming+retry benchmark script. action: schedule a scoping call next week to align the POC scope.
[11:18] Carlos Ruiz: great, we'll review and share our example prompts and qps numbers.
[11:25] Sophie Lee: i'll look at the security doc and follow up with any gaps.
[11:30] Aisha Patel: thanks everyone, i'll follow up via email with links and the deck.

End of transcript.
